Being treated badly predicted rising drinking — unless self-control was quick

Being belittled, excluded or treated unfairly reliably predicts heavy drinking — but not for everyone, and this team asked whether the difference lies in self-regulation. They followed 133 college students for three years, measuring alcohol problems annually alongside experiences of social mistreatment, and at the start put everyone through a task in an MRI scanner that measures how fast you can cancel an action already underway. Drinking problems rose across the three years, and rose more steeply for students reporting more mistreatment. Inhibition mattered too: students who could stop an action faster showed flatter drinking trajectories, and there was a significant interaction suggesting quicker self-control blunted the effect of being treated badly. Now the restraint. The key three-way test — whether inhibition changes how mistreatment shapes drinking over time — was not significant (p = 0.10). So the moderation shows up in the cross-section but is not confirmed in the trajectory, and the authors describe these analyses as exploratory, noting they did not correct for multiple comparisons. These were also relatively healthy college students rather than people with diagnosed alcohol use disorder.

Addiction Biology · Chia-Chuan Yu, et al. · September 2026

The invisible work of running a household: who carries it, and what it costs

"Mental load" names the part of running a household that leaves no trace: remembering the dentist appointment, noticing the shoes have got too small, holding the whole schedule in your head. Two German surveys — 368 women, then 1,871 mothers — separated that invisible work from the visible kind and asked what it costs. The split was stark. Women reported handling 84.2% of invisible tasks against 69.4% of visible ones, so the inequality is not in the cooking and cleaning but in the thinking behind them. They were also significantly more dissatisfied with how invisible work was divided — and that dissatisfaction belonged almost entirely to mothers, with women without children reporting essentially no difference between the two. The reasons given were consistent and revealing: the work is never finished and simply repeats, there is too much of it, and it leaves no break for yourself. Mental load tracked with worse mental health, correlating with negative affect, anxiety and depressive symptoms. Both studies are single snapshots, so nothing here establishes direction — and recruitment through parent forums and social media selects for women who already recognise the term.

PLOS One · Stefanie M. Jungmann, et al. · September 2026

Only 19.3% of Dutch forensic outpatients had a personality disorder diagnosis

In forensic mental health, a personality disorder diagnosis is not a label for its own sake — it shapes risk assessment, what treatment is offered, and how reoffending risk is managed. Researchers collected diagnoses for everyone treated in 2023 across fifteen Dutch outpatient forensic institutions, 10,560 people in total. A personality disorder was recorded for 19.3%: 12% as a primary diagnosis, 7.3% as an additional one. The authors read that as too low rather than reassuring, since reviews put rates in general psychiatric outpatient and detention settings considerably higher, and they conclude personality pathology is being under-recognised here. A second pattern supports them. Among those given a specific diagnosis, 71.2% were coded as "other specified" or unspecified — a placeholder rather than a description — with borderline and antisocial the only named categories above 2%. Diagnoses were more common among women, middle-aged patients, those in voluntary rather than mandated treatment, and those involved in more serious violent offences. The measurement caveat is large: institutions supplied data of differing completeness, and nothing was recorded about how any diagnosis was reached. This is a study of what gets written down.

Personality and Mental Health · Barbera E. Van Reijswoud, et al. · November 2026

A digital CBT programme cut nurse burnout. The suicide finding was weaker than billed.

Burnout and distress among nurses are severe enough to be called occupational epidemics, and screening programmes are the usual response — but screening identifies people, it does not treat them. This trial tested whether adding something helps. 501 at-risk nurses across US professional organizations and health systems were randomized to mental-health screening and referral alone, or the same plus MINDBODYSTRONG, a seven-session video-based cognitive-behavioural skills programme, then followed for six months. On anxiety, stress and healthy-lifestyle measures the added programme did better, though the effects were small. The clearest result was burnout: at six months, nurses in the programme had a significantly lower risk than those who got screening alone. Engagement was high, with 71% completing all seven sessions — though only 37% finished the skills activities that follow each one. On suicidal ideation, read carefully. Risk fell, and the six-month estimate looks substantial, but its confidence interval includes no effect at all. The authors' own results section says the suicidality effects did not reach statistical significance, while their conclusion describes reduced suicidal ideation and its potential life-saving impact. The burnout finding stands; the suicide claim does not yet.

Worldviews on Evidence-Based Nursing · Bernadette Mazurek Melnyk, et al. · October 2026

An AI therapist in VR matched ordinary CBT — with 20 students per group

If a language model can deliver CBT, the bottleneck of therapist availability in university counselling starts to look solvable. Researchers built a system combining virtual reality, a large language model and retrieval-augmented generation — a method that grounds the model's replies in a specific set of documents, here CBT material, rather than letting it improvise — and tested it against the real thing. Sixty students in Wuhan with academic anxiety were randomly assigned, twenty per arm, to the system, to face-to-face CBT, or to minimal support, for four weekly 50-minute sessions. Both active treatments beat minimal support on anxiety and on heart rate. Now the comparison everyone cares about, stated precisely: the difference between the two therapies was 2.05 points favouring traditional CBT, and it was not statistically significant (p = 0.103). That is not evidence they are equivalent — with twenty students per arm, this trial had no realistic power to detect a difference that size, so reading it as parity confuses "no difference found" with "no difference exists." The point estimate, if anything, favours the human. The authors call it preliminary and exploratory, and note it was not prospectively registered.

Frontiers in Public Health · Hao Fang, et al. · August 2026

ADHD medication varies sixfold across Danish towns. Nobody can explain why.

Whether a child is diagnosed with ADHD and prescribed medication ought to depend on the child. This study used Denmark's national registers — which cover every resident, with pharmacy records capturing every dispensed prescription regardless of who wrote it — to see whether it also depends on where they live. Across Danish municipalities in 2024, medication prevalence among 4-to-17-year-olds ranged from 9.6 per 1,000 children in parts of Funen to 58 per 1,000 in parts of North and Central Denmark, and diagnoses followed the same geography. The gap widened with age: among teenagers, diagnoses ranged from 22 to 113 per 1,000, meaning that in some municipalities more than one adolescent in ten carried a diagnosis while in others it was closer to one in forty-five. The interesting part is what failed to explain it. Municipal socioeconomic need showed only a borderline association with medication and none with diagnoses. Regional hospital waiting times showed nothing. Private child-psychiatrist capacity showed nothing. The authors caution that outcomes were measured across 98 municipalities while supply data existed only for 5 regions, which may itself explain the nulls.

Basic & Clinical Pharmacology & Toxicology · Heidi Sonne, et al. · October 2026

How many people fear dementia? After 56 studies, the answer is that we can't tell.

Fear of developing dementia shapes real behaviour: whether someone mentions memory lapses to a doctor, agrees to cognitive screening, or avoids the subject entirely. This review set out to establish how common that fear is among adults without a dementia diagnosis, searching eight databases including four Chinese-language ones and including 56 studies from China, Japan, South Korea, the US, the UK, Germany and Israel. The reported figures ranged from 12.7% to 68.0%. That spread is the finding, not a nuisance around it. The low figure came from a single-item question about severe fear put to German adults aged 40 to 70; the high one from scores on a dementia-fear scale among older adults in Chinese long-term care. Different constructs, instruments, cut-offs and populations — and the authors say plainly these should not be treated as comparable, concluding the evidence does not permit a reliable estimate. Their assessment of the measures explains why: most scales report internal consistency, but evidence that they mean the same thing across languages and cultures is limited or absent. What did hold up: anxiety and depression accompany greater fear, and social support less.

Frontiers in Public Health · Feng Chen, et al. · August 2026

After a first episode of psychosis, fewer than 1 in 5 kept taking the medication

A first episode of psychosis almost always ends with a prescription. What happens over the next year decides a lot. Researchers used US insurance claims from 2013 to 2021 to follow 11,889 people aged 15 to 40, from their first antipsychotic prescription onward. Adherence was measured as the share of days covered by a filled prescription across 365 days. 19.1% met the bar. That is fewer than one in five. Adherence was higher in schizophrenia than in other psychotic disorders, and higher again where a mood disorder was involved. People who were adherent had fewer emergency department visits and more outpatient behavioural health visits. Two cautions. A claims database records a pharmacy transaction, not a tablet taken, so the real figure is more likely lower than higher. And everyone here had twelve months of continuous private insurance, which leaves out much of the group where disengagement is worst. The direction isn't settled either, because people doing better may simply find it easier to keep filling a prescription. What the study does establish is the size of the gap. Four in five were not taking the medication that every plan for improving outcomes after a first episode quietly assumes they are.

JAMA network open · Emily Chi, et al. · September 2026

Teenagers with opioid use disorder got medication a fraction as often as adults

One in a hundred American teenagers and young adults has an opioid use disorder. There are medications that reduce the risk of dying from it. Researchers used Medicaid claims from every US state, 2016 to 2023, to follow 229,847 people aged 13 to 25 with the diagnosis. Half started treatment within two weeks. A third stayed long enough to count as engaged. Of those, 46% received medication. Then the age split. Among under-18s who had engaged in treatment, 6.6% received medication. Among over-18s in the same system, 51.2% did. A teenager who made it to treatment was roughly eight times less likely to be offered the thing that works. Overall, 3.1%, about one in 32, stayed on medication for six months, which is the national quality benchmark. Retention was best on methadone. The youngest adolescents and racially minoritised young people fell out earliest at every stage. These are billing records, so engagement is an administrative category, not a clinical one. But the yardstick is the system's own national quality measure. Measured against the standard the system set for itself, it is failing the youngest patients most, and failing them earliest.

JAMA network open · Scott E Hadland, et al. · October 2026

From zero adverse childhood experiences to six, suicidal thinking went from 6% to 41%

Most of what we know about adverse childhood experiences comes from adults remembering their childhoods, using a checklist that ignores anything outside the home. This study did it differently: 1,850 young people from schools in the southern US, assessed at around 19, counting both conventional adversities and community-level ones like discrimination. The associations are graded. Each step up carries more harm. Depression: 21% at zero adverse experiences, 46% at four to five, 57% at six or more. PTSD: 2%, then 15%, then 31%. Suicidal thinking: 6%, then 28%, then 41%. Academic achievement and college attendance fell as exposure rose. Ten of fourteen adversity types mattered independently. The four most consistent were emotional abuse, sexual abuse, witnessing domestic violence, and discrimination. That last one isn't on the standard checklist. The limits: several exposures and outcomes were measured at the same time, so this is association, not proof of cause. And one region is not a country. What it does show is that adversity accumulates, that the climb is gradual rather than sudden, and that what counts as adversity may need widening.

JAMA network open · Jeff R Temple, et al. · September 2026

Psychodynamic therapy for schizophrenia finally got a proper trial. It worked.

Psychodynamic therapy has been used with people with schizophrenia for decades, mostly on clinical conviction rather than evidence. This trial tested it. At a Berlin hospital, 130 outpatients with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder were randomly assigned to modified psychodynamic psychotherapy, at least 30 sessions, plus usual care, or usual care alone. The primary outcome was psychosocial functioning. The therapy group did better at 24 months, and the gap was slightly wider at 36 months than at the end of treatment. Adverse events were similar across groups. Two participants died by suicide, one in each arm. Read it with the design in mind. It is a single centre. Assessors were blinded, but participants and therapists knew which arm they were in, which matters when the outcome is a rated judgement of functioning. Anyone whose substance use needed its own treatment was excluded, which removes a large part of a real caseload. The authors also state that people with lived experience were not involved in designing or reporting it. Stating that is unusual. It is the kind of limitation most trials leave unmentioned rather than printed in their own abstract.

The lancet. Psychiatry · Christiane Montag, et al. · October 2026

Blood-pressure drugs were a promising alcohol treatment. In two large cohorts, they did nothing.

Alcohol use disorder has few effective medications, so a new lead matters. L-type calcium channel blockers, normally prescribed for blood pressure, had genetic and laboratory evidence behind them. This study checked whether that survived contact with actual patients. Two preregistered cohort studies, one in the US Veterans Affairs system and one at Kaiser Permanente. People newly started on a brain-penetrant version were compared with people started on a similar drug that does not cross into the brain, and with people taking neither. The outcome was change in drinks per week. In the VA: a difference of 0.14 drinks per week, with a confidence interval spanning zero. Against unexposed patients: exactly 0.00. Kaiser gave the same answer. Subgroups pointed the same way. This is observational, so it cannot rule out what a trial might find, and people prescribed one blood-pressure drug rather than another differ in ways matching only partly fixes. But two independent systems, preregistered, both finding nothing, is itself a finding. Their recommendation is to stop pursuing this target and spend the effort elsewhere, which is exactly what a null result is for.

Pharmacoepidemiology and drug safety · Christopher T Rentsch, et al. · October 2026

An online therapy for teen depression beat usual care, and missed its own threshold for mattering

Behavioural activation suits digital delivery. It is structured, it is largely about scheduling activity, and it leans less on a long therapeutic relationship. 219 adolescents with mild to moderate depression were randomised to therapist-guided internet behavioural activation, a self-guided version, or treatment as usual. Ten weeks. Blinded raters at three months. Depression scores fell 17.0 points with a therapist, 16.0 self-guided, and 11.6 with usual care. Both digital groups ended below the clinical cut-off. Therapist-guided beat usual care by 4.68 points. p=0.048. The confidence interval runs from 0.05 to 9.30, which only just clears zero. Now the part worth sitting with. Before the trial began, the researchers set six points as the smallest difference that would count as clinically important. The result did not reach it. Significance also disappeared under a different modelling choice. Both digital options cost less than usual care. The authors' own verdict: symptoms fell, importance and robustness uncertain. A trial that clears statistical significance and misses its own clinical threshold is not a failed trial. It is an honestly reported one, which is rarer than it should be.

BMJ mental health · Rebecca Andersson, et al. · August 2026

A short burst of exercise cut alcohol craving. The whole evidence base is six studies.

Craving is one of the more tractable targets in problematic drinking. It fluctuates, so in principle it can be interrupted. Exercise has been proposed as one way to do that. This systematic review searched four databases for studies where young adults aged 18 to 29 with problematic drinking had craving measured after a single bout of exercise. Six studies met the criteria. Pooled, acute exercise reduced craving with a Hedges' g of about 0.55, conventionally a moderate effect, with moderate variation between studies. The reviewers also noted reductions in anxiety, changes in stress markers, and improvements in executive function, though these varied a lot. The honest framing is the size of the evidence base, not the size of the effect. Six small studies is very few, and a pooled effect drawn from that many is unstable: one more trial pointing the other way would move it. A single session also says nothing about whether drinking changes, which is the outcome that matters. The review's own conclusion is a call for better trials, not a recommendation to prescribe exercise for craving. Read it as a hypothesis worth testing properly.

European journal of sport science · P Sampedro-Piquero, et al. · October 2026

Long-term psychodynamic therapy for depression earned a Strong recommendation and a very-low-certainty rating, in the same paper

Long-term psychodynamic therapy is expensive in both time and money, so whether it beats shorter or different treatments is a real question. This preregistered meta-analysis found 16 randomised trials, 1,992 people, every one of them at least nine months and 30 sessions. Against all comparators, the pooled effect on depressive symptoms was a standardised mean difference of 0.34. Against active treatments specifically, 0.27. Both modest. Gains generally held at follow-up. A subgroup comparison against active controls gave a bigger number, 0.61 - and this is where care is needed. That subgroup had more heterogeneity, and the authors rate its certainty very low. So the same paper issues a Strong recommendation for reducing depressive symptoms, and a Weak one for the comparison against active alternatives. Risk of bias was a concern in most trials. The fair reading is neither headline alone. It works, modestly, on evidence that is weakest exactly where you would want it strongest. Risk of bias was flagged in most of the sixteen trials, and there were too few of them to examine who actually benefits most.

Depression and anxiety · Max Moser, et al. · September 2026

A 17-minute video shown during a forensic exam lowered acute stress. Fifty women took part.

Three-quarters of sexual assault survivors meet criteria for PTSD a month later. The forensic medical examination is often the only moment the health system reliably has with them. This trial tested whether that moment could carry an intervention. Across four US examination programmes, women assaulted within the past week were randomised at the exam to a 17-minute video - social support, mindfulness, gradual self-exposure - or to usual care. A week later, those still above threshold were randomised again to a three-week daily text programme, or not. Fifty women took part. Those assigned the video had lower odds of acute stress, odds ratio 0.13. They also reported less pain at one week. Now the caution. Fifty people. That odds ratio has a confidence interval running from 0.02 to 0.78, which is consistent with an enormous effect or a modest one. Follow-up was four weeks, which cannot speak to PTSD at three months. This is what a pilot is for: showing a bigger trial is worth running. It also shows the forensic examination can carry an intervention at all, which was not obvious, and which is the part a larger study can build on.

JAMA network open · Kate Walsh, et al. · September 2026

Three ways of detecting hazardous drinking found three different groups of patients

Asking people how much they drink is the standard screen, and it is known to be imperfect. PEth is a blood marker reflecting the past few weeks, sometimes treated as the objective answer. This study compared them in Swedish primary care records: 3,679 patients with both a questionnaire and a PEth test, and 8,934 with a PEth test and a recorded weekly intake. The three methods disagreed. The AUDIT questionnaire flagged 26.5% as hazardous. PEth flagged 14.6% and 18.3% across the two samples. Self-reported weekly drinks flagged 8.5%. And each method found people the other two missed. The disagreement isn't random. At the same PEth level, men and patients with more education or income reported drinking more, while younger patients scored higher on the questionnaire. So the blood test is not a lie detector for what someone tells you. The authors' conclusion: read it alongside the self-report, not instead of it. Each method answers a slightly different question: what someone drank, what they will say they drank, and what their blood still holds. Together they find more risk than any one alone.

Annals of family medicine · Viktor Månsson, et al. · September 2026

In 182 Spanish court cases involving mania, bipolar disorder fully excused the defendant 3.3% of the time

Spanish law recognises bipolar disorder as something that can reduce or remove criminal responsibility. How often it actually does is a separate question. Researchers reviewed five years of Spanish criminal sentences involving manic symptoms. They found 182 and went through each one. The defendants were mostly male, and strikingly isolated. 77% lacked family support. 69% already had a bipolar diagnosis before the offence. But at the time of the offence, 62% were on no medication and 64% had no psychiatric follow-up. Nearly two-thirds had a prior criminal record. The outcomes surprise people who assume a mental health defence usually works. The commonest results were a dismissed appeal and a prison sentence. Court-ordered treatment happened in 6.6% of cases. Bipolar disorder fully excused the defendant in 3.3% - six cases out of 182. This cannot tell you how often people with bipolar disorder offend, which is a different and much smaller number. What it does show is a population mostly diagnosed and mostly untreated at the point things went wrong, which points at services rather than at courts.

International journal of law and psychiatry · Covadonga Canga-Espina, et al. · June 2026

Overdose is the leading cause of maternal death. Staying on medication halved the risk.

Overdose is the leading cause of maternal death in the US, and the year after birth is when it happens. Researchers used Tennessee Medicaid records linked to birth and death certificates to follow 9,360 pregnancies among people receiving medication for opioid use disorder. They counted the days of medication actually dispensed between 90 days before delivery and 41 days after, then watched what happened from six weeks to one year post partum. 1.58% died or overdosed within that year. The median time to it was 186 days - about six months after birth, long after most postpartum care has ended. Longer time on medication went with lower risk. At the full 132 days, the adjusted hazard ratio was 0.52 against a single day. This is observational, and that matters. People who stay on treatment differ from those who stop in housing, support and illness severity, in ways no statistical adjustment fully fixes. What is not in doubt is when the danger peaks. Six months after delivery is well past the end of most postpartum care, and the medication window that mattered had closed long before.

JAMA network open · Ahra Kim, et al. · October 2026

In a forensic hospital study, violence clustered in the periods when treatment had stopped

The overall crime rate among people with schizophrenia is not meaningfully higher than the general population's. So the useful question is not whether the diagnosis carries risk, but which circumstances do. Korean researchers reviewed records from a national forensic hospital, comparing 55 patients with schizophrenia who had committed homicide with 49 who had been violent without killing. The finding that applies to both groups is the important one. Most violent acts happened during periods when treatment had stopped, and were most commonly driven by persecutory delusions. Both groups frequently had little social support and a history of childhood trauma or later victimisation. The two groups differed in pattern, not in kind - one more premeditated and in private, the other more impulsive and in public. The limits are real: one hospital, about a hundred patients, reviewed retrospectively, and everyone in it had already been violent. It cannot estimate risk in the wider population, and should not be read as doing so. The usable finding is narrower and more practical: among people who had already become violent, the violence clustered where treatment had stopped.

Journal of Korean medical science · Yujin Lee, et al. · August 2026

A phase 3 trial tested an app against the symptoms of schizophrenia no drug is approved for

Negative symptoms of schizophrenia - blunted motivation, reduced pleasure, withdrawal - drive much of the long-term disability. No drug is approved in the US to treat them. CONVOKE was a phase 3, double-blind trial at 66 US sites. 457 adults already on antipsychotics were randomised to an investigational smartphone therapeutic or to a digital control app, for 16 weeks. The measure was motivation and pleasure. Both groups improved. The treatment arm by 6.8 points, the control app by 4.2. The difference was 2.6 points, p below 0.001. Three things to hold together. The design is genuinely strong: double-blind, a sham app rather than a waiting list, large, phase 3. The effect is modest. And the control arm improved substantially by itself, which is both what a good sham looks like and a reminder of how much of a digital intervention's benefit is attention and structure. Industry-developed and industry-funded - normal at this stage, still worth saying. If it reaches clinics it would be the first thing specifically approved for symptoms that currently have no approved treatment at all. That is the context the modest effect sits in.

JAMA network open · Abhishek Pratap, et al. · September 2026

Twenty-five years of US data suggest filicide is not one crime but four

Filicide is rare enough that most research on it rests on small samples. That is a poor basis for the risk assessments and prevention programmes built on top of it. This study used 25 years of US police-reported incident data, 1999 to 2023, covering 3,974 incidents - and split them by the age of the child. Four categories: within 24 hours of birth, the first year, ages one to seventeen, and adult children. The categories differed significantly on offender age, offender sex, race, method and victim characteristics. Cases involving newborns were most often associated with younger female offenders. Cases involving adult children typically involved older male offenders and firearms. The authors' argument follows: one prevention framework applied across all four is unlikely to fit any of them well. The limits are those of police data. Incidents are recorded as reported, coverage is incomplete, and the maternal mental health information that would matter most clinically is not in this dataset at all. What it offers is scale on a question where nearly everything else is small, and a reason to stop treating four very different situations as one category.

Journal of interpersonal violence · Jeffrey A Walsh, et al. · October 2026

When a weapon was involved in partner violence, panic and PTSD followed. Depression did not.

A weapon in intimate partner violence signals lethality in a way other violence may not. Whether that leaves a distinct mental health signature is hard to test, because weapon-involved violence rarely happens on its own. Researchers followed 1,114 Australian women across six waves, from antenatal clinics onward, measuring symptoms of depression, panic, PTSD and separation anxiety each time. Over the follow-up, 43 women reported weapon-involved violence, 171 non-weapon physical violence, and 726 psychological abuse. The models adjusted for the other violence happening at the same time, for past violence, and for each woman's own earlier symptoms. After all that, weapon involvement still predicted panic and PTSD symptoms. It did not predict depression or separation anxiety. The specificity is the point. Not a general worsening, but a pattern concentrated in fear-based conditions - which is what you would expect if the mechanism runs through threat to life. The caution: 43 women is a small exposed group, and the intervals are wide. The cohort also began in antenatal clinics, so it is not a general population sample. What survives adjustment is a pattern worth looking for clinically, not a prevalence estimate.

Dissociation - detachment from your own experience, body, or sense of self - is common in psychosis and tracks with clinical risk. Nobody had quantified how severe it usually is. This review searched six databases, extracted data on 22 measures, and meta-analysed the four with enough datasets. The Dissociative Experiences Scale, the biggest with 51 datasets and 3,878 people, pooled to a mean of 21.28. Moderately elevated. The depersonalisation scale pooled high too, and both scoring methods for anomalous self-experience showed clinically relevant levels. But the number that matters is none of those. Heterogeneity was above 85%. The studies disagree with each other far more than chance explains, which means the pooled average describes almost no individual patient. The authors say it plainly: dissociation is not uniform in this population. Read properly, that is an argument for assessing it in each person rather than assuming a typical level - because the review's strongest finding is that there isn't one. An average built from studies that disagree this much is a summary of a literature, not a description of a patient.

274 social science findings were re-run. One study and one replication still cannot settle it.

The SCORE project re-ran 274 findings from business, economics, education, political science, psychology and sociology, and applied thirteen different methods for judging whether each replication succeeded. This paper asked a prior question: do those methods actually work? Largely, no. At the sample sizes typical of an original study and one replication, the methods cannot reliably decide. There isn't enough information in two studies, however you arrange the arithmetic. Which means a headline saying something 'failed to replicate' is often as uncertain as the finding it is judging. The second part is more useful. Combining the original with its replication, using estimators that correct for bias in the original, performed close to unbiased - and those combined estimates landed substantially closer to the replication than to the original. That is the signature of published findings being inflated. But the null was still rejected in 59% to 81% of pairs. So: not mostly nothing. Mostly smaller than first reported. The practical advice is unglamorous and good: check that a method for judging replication behaves sensibly on your data before trusting what it tells you.

In borderline personality disorder, self-contempt fell and something else moved in to replace it

Self-contempt is a recognisable feature of borderline personality disorder and a plausible target for therapy. It is usually measured by asking - which is exactly the self-report someone deep in self-contempt may answer unreliably. This study watched instead. 79 people: 27 clients with BPD in good psychiatric management, 23 in treatment as usual, and 29 healthy controls. Everyone did structured two-chair dialogues about self-criticism at two time points, outside the therapy room, rated from video. Observed self-contempt fell with a large effect in the structured treatment - close to the level of healthy controls - and a medium effect in treatment as usual. The more interesting result is what replaced it. Clients in the structured treatment increasingly reached self-compassion and assertive anger. That did not happen in treatment as usual, or in the healthy controls, who had less room to move. Undoing self-contempt may not be subtraction. It may be making space. Small groups, four months, and a staged task rather than a real session. But watching what someone does with self-criticism, instead of asking them to rate it, is the methodological point worth borrowing.

Most trauma therapy trials follow people for a year, and most are delivered by specialists in well-resourced settings. This one is neither. 63 South African adolescents with PTSD were randomised to prolonged exposure or supportive counselling. Both were delivered by newly trained nurses with no prior psychotherapy experience. The protocol averaged nine sessions. This report adds a five-year follow-up to data already published at 3, 6, 12 and 24 months. Both groups kept a significant reduction in PTSD symptoms all the way to 60 months. Now the careful part. Prolonged exposure did better at every earlier follow-up. At five years it no longer did - p was 0.28, with a small-to-moderate effect still pointing its way. That is not the same as the advantage vanishing. In a trial of 63 people, the power to detect a modest difference at the final timepoint is limited. What survived is the headline: nine sessions, non-specialist staff, still working five years on. Where specialists are scarce, a protocol that works in nine sessions delivered by nurses is worth more than a better one nobody can staff.

A meta-analysis of drug-cue brain imaging found one reliable cluster, and it was not the striatum

Showing someone pictures of their drug and watching the brain respond is a central paradigm in addiction neuroscience. The usual summary involves a hyperreactive reward circuit centred on the striatum. This meta-analysis tested how well that holds. It pooled case-control contrasts - how people with a substance use disorder differ from controls viewing the same cues - which avoids some confounds that trouble within-group designs. One reliable cluster emerged: the ventral anterior cingulate cortex, where reward pathways meet the default-mode network. Reliable striatal convergence was not observed. The cluster was context-dependent in a telling way. Against neutral cues, the effect held no matter how long someone had been abstinent. Against natural rewards - food, money, faces - it declined with longer abstinence. Contributions were also sensitive to whether comparison images matched for human content. A face in a photograph does work of its own. None of this says cues don't matter. It says the clean reward-centre story isn't what the data converge on. It also says the comparison image is doing more work than the field usually acknowledges, which is a design problem rather than a brain finding.
